We need to answer a complex multi-step question. The user wants:

1) Identify local authorities that did NOT see an overall decrease in amount of households since 2011 (i.e., households increased or stable) according to Welsh Census 2021 and official Welsh government data. So we need list of local authorities where household numbers did not decrease between 2011 and 2021.

2) From those local authorities, filter to those that had a population less than 120,000 at mid-year 2021 and are not in North Wales region.

3) From this selection, identify the local authorities that have seen an increase of over 2% in people aged 25-44 between mid-year 2021 and mid-year 2022.

So need data:

- Household change 2011-2021 per local authority.
- Population mid-year 2021 per local authority (to filter <120,000). Also location region to exclude North Wales (North Wales includes: Conwy, Denbighshire, Flintshire, Gwynedd, Wrexham? Actually North Wales region comprises Conwy, Denbighshire, Flintshire, Gwynedd, Wrexham? Many definitions: North Wales division includes Conwy, Denbighshire, Flintshire, Gwynedd, Wrexham. Might also include maybe some others. We'll use standard: Conwy, Denbighshire, Flintshire, Gwynedd, Wrexham.

- 25-44 age group increase >2% between mid-year 2021 and mid-year 2022 per local authority.

Thus we need datasets.

We already have sources:

- Household change paper: "The number of households has increased by almost 44,000 since 2011... All but three local authorities in Wales saw an increase in the number of households... The areas where there were decreases in the number of households were Gwynedd (2.6% decrease), Ceredigion (2.1% decrease) and Blaenau Gwent (0.4% decrease)." This is from page lines above. The households data maybe available.

So which local authorities did not see a decrease? Everyone except Gwynedd, Ceredigion, Blaenau Gwent had increases. So list of all 22 local authorities minus those 3 = 19.

- Population mid-year 2021 for each local authority: We have a table from the PDF eight (source). It lists populations for each local authority: Cardiff 362,308 ; Swansea 238,490 ; Rhondda Cynon Taf 237,651 ; Carmarthenshire 187,897 ; Caerphilly 175,952 ; Newport 159,592 ; Flintshire 154,962 ; Bridgend 145,488 ; Neath Port Talbot 142,289 ; Wrexham 135,117 ; Powys 133,169 ; Vale of Glamorgan 131,939 ; Pembrokeshire 123,360 ; Gwynedd 117,393 ; Conwy 114,741 ; Denbighshire 95,817 ; Monmouthshire 92,957 ; Torfaen 92,276 ; Ceredigion 71,475 ; Isle of Anglesey 68,878 ; Blaenau Gwent 66,904 ; Merthyr Tydfil 58,836.

Need those with population <120,000: So we need those below 120k. These are: Pembrokeshire 123360 is >120k, so excluded. Powys 133k excluded. Rhondda Cynon 237k excluded. etc. So we include local authorities with <120k: list:

- Cardiff? >120k, exclude. Actually Cardiff 362k >120k. Swansea 238k >120k. Rhondda Cynon 237k >120k. Carmarthenshire 187k >120k. Caerphilly 175k >120k. Newport 159k >120k. Flintshire 154k >120k. Bridgend 145k >120k. Neath Port Talbot 142k >120k. Wrexham 135k >120k. Powys 133k >120k. Vale of Glamorgan 132k >120k. Pembrokeshire 123k >120k. Gwynedd 117k <120k. Conwy 114k <120k. Denbighshire 95k <120k. Monmouthshire 92k <120k. Torfaen 92k <120k. Ceredigion 71k <120k. Isle of Anglesey 68k <120k. Blaenau Gwent 66k <120k. Merthyr Tydfil 58k <120k. So local authorities with <120k: Gwynedd, Conwy, Denbighshire, Monmouthshire, Torfaen, Ceredigion, Isle of Anglesey, Blaenau Gwent, Merthyr Tydfil. Also maybe it includes other ones? Check if there are any others slightly below 120: not.

Now among these, exclude North Wales region. North Wales region comprises Conwy, Denbighshire, Flintshire, Gwynedd, Wrexham. (Also maybe Anglesey is sometimes considered North Wales). For safety, exclude Conwy, Denbighshire, Gwynedd. So remaining: Monmouthshire, Torfaen, Ceredigion, Isle of Anglesey, Blaenau Gwent, Merthyr Tydfil.

But we also must check that these local authorities had household numbers that did NOT decrease. Household decrease list: Gwynedd, Ceredigion, Blaenau Gwent. So Ceredigion and Blaenau Gwent had decreases. Thus we need to exclude them. So after exclusion we get: Monmouthshire, Torfaen, Isle of Anglesey, Merthyr Tydfil. Wait Isle of Anglesey was in North Wales? It's in North Wales historically. It's considered part of North Wales region (Anglesey). So exclude it too. So we are left with Monmouthshire and Torfaen. But we need to confirm if Isle of Anglesey considered North Wales; yes, it is part of North Wales county. So remove. We then have Monmouthshire, Torfaen.

Need to verify whether households for Monmouthshire and Torfaen increased: Check earlier list: household decrease list did not include them. So they increased. Good.

Now we need to see which of these had >2% increase in people aged 25-44 between mid-year 2021 and mid-year 2022.

We need data for that.

We need mid-year 2021 25-44 population per local authority, and mid-year 2022 25-44 population per local authority. Then compute percent change.

Source: Stats Wales dataset "Population estimates by local authority, year, sex and age" includes age by single year. We can use dataset to get 25-44 aggregated age groups. Might require calculation. But we can glean from published summary? Might be in a bulletin.

## Main information
Designation Accredited official statistics
Data provider Office for National Statistics (ONS)
Data source Mid-year population estimates
Dataset ID 82d9faea-b515-41cd-aedb-8f4594f66ce5

## Overview
Summary of dataset and variables  
This dataset provides population estimates for the local authorities in Wales, the English regions and the UK countries for the period from 1991 onwards by sex and single year of age.
It should be noted that for mid-2020 there are some definitional changes, particularly affecting the migration components, compared with mid-2019 population estimates data and it is advised users read the Quality and Methodology Information section on the Office for National Statistics website.
For Wales, England and Northern Ireland, the mid-2021 population estimates are the first population estimates to be based on the 2021 censuses for these countries. For Scotland, the census was moved to 2022. The mid-2022 population estimates are the first population estimates to be based on the 2022 Census for Scotland.
On 23 November 2023, the data set from 2012 to 2020 for Wales and England were rebased to be consistent with the results of Census 2021. Northern Ireland published rebased 2012 to 2020 data on 29 June 2023. Scotland published rebased 2012 to 2020 data on 9 July 2024.
On 29 July 2026 estimates for mid-2022, mid-2023 and mid-2024 were revised by the ONS to account for updated estimates of international migration for Wales and England.
Internal migration estimates for mid-2023 have been produced using a different method to previous years, following a change to the variables available in the Higher Education Statistics Agency data.
Data collection or calculation  
The Office for National Statistics (ONS) publish mid-year population estimates for Wales and England as a whole. Further information on how the data are calculated can be found on the ONS' website. A link can be found in the weblink section.

## Overview
Summary of dataset and variables  
This dataset provides population estimates for the local authorities in Wales, the English regions and the UK countries for the period from 1991 onwards by sex and single year of age.
It should be noted that for mid-2020 there are some definitional changes, particularly affecting the migration components, compared with mid-2019 population estimates data and it is advised users read the Quality and Methodology Information section on the Office for National Statistics website.
For Wales, England and Northern Ireland, the mid-2021 population estimates are the first population estimates to be based on the 2021 censuses for these countries. For Scotland, the census was moved to 2022. The mid-2022 population estimates are the first population estimates to be based on the 2022 Census for Scotland.
On 23 November 2023, the data set from 2012 to 2020 for Wales and England were rebased to be consistent with the results of Census 2021. Northern Ireland published rebased 2012 to 2020 data on 29 June 2023. Scotland published rebased 2012 to 2020 data on 9 July 2024.
On 29 July 2026 estimates for mid-2022, mid-2023 and mid-2024 were revised by the ONS to account for updated estimates of international migration for Wales and England.
Internal migration estimates for mid-2023 have been produced using a different method to previous years, following a change to the variables available in the Higher Education Statistics Agency data.

8.1.Population forecasts  
Population forecasts are essential for service planning, both in terms of being able to  
plan for increases or decreases in population size but also to be aware of, and  
mitigate for, the nuances and needs of a changing age structure.  
The Cambridgeshire County Council Policy and Insight Team publish population  
forecasts based on births, deaths, migration and known housing developments in  
Cambridgeshire and Peterborough. This section presents the data from the 2022-  
based population forecasts available on Cambridgeshire & Peterborough Insight.  9
Cambridgeshire  
Between 2022 and 2031 the population of Cambridgeshire is forecast to increase  
from 689,530 people to 769,135 people, an increase of just over 79,600 (11.5%).  
The rate of increase in the subsequent 10 years to 2041 is slower with an extra

population forecasts between 2031 and 2041.  
Age band  
Over the 9 years to 2031 is it forecast that there will be decreases in the number of  
children and young people aged 5 to 14 years (1,365 children, 1.7%) and people  
aged in their fifties (2,330 people, 2.5%) in Cambridgeshire, with notable increases  
expected in all other age bands, especially in the older age groups. An increase is

Between 2022 and 2031 the population of Peterborough is forecast to increase from  
218,130 people to 234,540 people, an increase of over 16,400 (7.5%). The rate of

## [PDF page 45]
Appendices  
Appendix 1: Methodology for determining types of  
development  
There is no perfect fit between Census geographies and the planning boundaries of  
new developments. This analysis uses a best fit look up methodology applying  
Census 2011 and Census 2021 Output Area (OA) geographies to the planning  
boundaries of the new developments.  
The methodology differs slightly between those new developments classified as  
'Older new developments' (where notable development began prior to Census 2011),  
and those classified as 'New developments' (where notable development has begun  
between Census 2011 and Census 2021).  
The best fit look up methodology means that OAs included will cover areas that lie  
outside the planning boundary.  
Older New Developments  
  New developments where notable dwelling build began prior to Census 2011.  
  Inclusion of all Census 2021 Output Areas that lie within or intersect the planning  
boundary of the new development.  
  Inclusion of all Census 2011 Output Areas that lie within or intersect the planning  
boundary of the new development.  
  Inclusion of additional Census 2021 OAs or Census 2011 OAs to ensure that the  
geographical area covered is consistent across the two sets of geographies,  
allowing for Census 2011 to Census 2021 change over time comparison.  
New developments  
  New developments where notable dwelling build began between Census 2011  
and Census 2021.  
  Analysis of Census 2021 Output Areas that lie within or intersect the planning  
boundary of the new development.  
  Where the Census 2021 OA intersects but does not lie completely within the  
planning boundary of the new development, an analysis of overlap by count of  
address points has been undertaken. Of these, only those OAs where more than  
50% of the address points lie within the planning boundary have been included.  
Future new developments  
  Those new developments where dwelling build is limited so far or not yet started.  
  Inclusion of all Census 2021 Output Areas that lie within or intersect the planning  
boundary of the new development.  
Additional note:

## [PDF page 45]
45

## [PDF page 46]
In some cases, the boundaries of Census 2021 OAs span more than one new  
development, for example where developments are close or neighbouring such as  
Loves Farm and Wintringham Park. For ‘Older new developments’ these OAs have  
been included, even if a greater number of address points sit outside the new  
development planning boundary than within. This is to enable comparison over time  
with Census 2011 data on a like for like basis.  
Where OAs of 'Older new developments' or 'New developments' span the planning  
boundaries of 'Future new developments', the OA has been assigned to the relevant  
'Older new development' or 'New development' as building has yet to substantially  
commence for the 'Future new development' sites.
46

Appendices  
Appendix 1: Methodology for determining types of  
development  
There is no perfect fit between Census geographies and the planning boundaries of  
new developments. This analysis uses a best fit look up methodology applying  
Census 2011 and Census 2021 Output Area (OA) geographies to the planning  
boundaries of the new developments.  
The methodology differs slightly between those new developments classified as  
'Older new developments' (where notable development began prior to Census 2011),  
and those classified as 'New developments' (where notable development has begun  
between Census 2011 and Census 2021).  
The best fit look up methodology means that OAs included will cover areas that lie  
outside the planning boundary.  
Older New Developments  
  New developments where notable dwelling build began prior to Census 2011.  
  Inclusion of all Census 2021 Output Areas that lie within or intersect the planning  
boundary of the new development.  
  Inclusion of all Census 2011 Output Areas that lie within or intersect the planning  
boundary of the new development.  
  Inclusion of additional Census 2021 OAs or Census 2011 OAs to ensure that the  
geographical area covered is consistent across the two sets of geographies,  
allowing for Census 2011 to Census 2021 change over time comparison.  
New developments  
  New developments where notable dwelling build began between Census 2011  
and Census 2021.  
  Analysis of Census 2021 Output Areas that lie within or intersect the planning  
boundary of the new development.  
  Where the Census 2021 OA intersects but does not lie completely within the  
planning boundary of the new development, an analysis of overlap by count of  
address points has been undertaken. Of these, only those OAs where more than  
50% of the address points lie within the planning boundary have been included.  
Future new developments  
  Those new developments where dwelling build is limited so far or not yet started.  
  Inclusion of all Census 2021 Output Areas that lie within or intersect the planning  
boundary of the new development.
